# 2 Maccabees Chapter 14 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 14 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_014_page_001.jpg

---

## Council Notes

**Chapter Overview:** Demetrius I, Alcimus's treachery, Nicanor's complex relationship with Judas, and the death of Razis (vv. 37-46). The Razis passage is one of the most violent deaths in any ancient text and is presented as heroic, noble martyrdom. The author uses it immediately before the final battle with Nicanor. Do not soften any element of the death scene.

**Key Decisions:**

**Razis Passage (vv. 37-46):**
- "Father of the Jews" (v. 37): Greek *patēr tōn Ioudaiōn* — retain as an honorific title; all three agree
- "Times of separation / mingling" (v. 38): Greek *akrasia* and *kraseis* — period when Jews were forced to intermingle with Gentile culture; EMET "no mingling," LOGOS "no intermingling," PNEUMA "no forced mixing" — LOGOS preferred
- "Fell upon his own sword" (LOGOS v. 41): Greek *epespasato tēn machairan*: drew/unsheathed his sword and fell on it — LOGOS rendering correct; EMET is ambiguous
- "Noble birth" (v. 42): Greek *eugeneia*: nobility/noble birth — retain; PNEUMA substitutes "noble character" — too psychological; the term is about lineage
- "Threw himself down...into the crowd" (v. 43): Greek *katepēdēsen eis tous ochlous*: leaped/threw himself down into the crowds — the act is deliberate; retain "threw himself down"
- "Entirely drained of blood" (v. 46): Greek *to haima katakechymenon*: completely emptied of blood — retain the physical specificity
- "Tore out his entrails" (v. 46): Greek *ta splagchna protinoumenos*: pulling out / drawing forth the entrails — do NOT sanitize; EMET/LOGOS "tore out his entrails" is correct
- "Hurled them at the crowd" (v. 46): Greek *epirripsen tois ochlois*: threw/hurled at the crowds — retain; PNEUMA "hurled them with both hands into the crowd" is acceptable
- "Lord of life and spirit" (v. 46): Greek *ton despotēn tēs zōēs kai tou pneumatos*: master/lord of life and spirit — retain exactly; this is a theological title

**Other Decisions:**
- "Hasideans" (v. 6): Greek *Asidaioi* — retain as a proper group name; all three agree
- "Holy altar" vs. "sacred altar" (v. 3): SOPHIA "holy altar"
- Nicanor's threat (v. 33): all three render the Dionysus temple threat clearly; retain

---

**14:1** Three years later, word reached Judas and his men that Demetrius son of Seleucus had sailed into the harbor at Tripolis with a strong army and a fleet

**14:2** and had seized the kingdom, after making away with Antiochus and his guardian Lysias.

**14:3** Now a certain Alcimus, who had formerly been high priest and had deliberately defiled himself in the time of the mingling with the Gentiles, realized that no means of safety was left to him and no further access to the holy altar.

**14:4** He came to King Demetrius in the one hundred and fifty-first year, bringing him a golden crown, a palm branch, and besides these some of the customary olive branches from the temple. On that day he kept silent.

**14:5** But having found a fitting moment for his mad scheme, when he was invited into Demetrius's council and was questioned about the attitude and purposes of the Jews, he answered:

**14:6** "Those among the Jews who are called Hasideans, whose leader is Judas Maccabeus, are maintaining a state of war and stirring up sedition, and will not let the kingdom have peace.

**14:7** Therefore, robbed of my ancestral honor — I mean the high priesthood — I have come here,

**14:8** first out of genuine concern for the king's interests, and second out of regard for my own countrymen; for through the folly of the men I mentioned, our whole nation is in serious trouble.

**14:9** I urge you therefore, O king, having informed yourself of all these matters, to take thought for our country and our nation, which is beset on every side, in accordance with the gracious goodwill you show to all.

**14:10** For as long as Judas is alive, it is impossible for the government to find peace."

**14:11** When he had said this, the rest of the king's friends, who were hostile to Judas, quickly inflamed Demetrius further.

**14:12** He immediately appointed Nicanor, who had been in command of the elephants, as governor of Judea, and sent him off

**14:13** with orders to kill Judas, scatter his men, and install Alcimus as high priest of the great temple.

**14:14** The Gentiles throughout Judea who had previously fled from Judas began flocking to Nicanor, thinking that the misfortunes and calamities of the Jews would serve their own interests.

**14:15** When the Jews heard of Nicanor's coming and the gathering of the Gentiles, they threw earth on their heads and entreated him who had established his people for ever and who always upholds his inheritance by his appearing.

**14:16** At the command of their leader, they moved out at once and met the enemy at a village called Dessau.

**14:17** Simon, the brother of Judas, had engaged Nicanor but suffered a temporary reverse owing to the unexpected appearance of the enemy.

**14:18** Nevertheless, Nicanor, hearing of the valor of Judas and his men and the courage with which they fought for their fatherland, was reluctant to settle the matter by bloodshed.

**14:19** So he sent Posidonius, Theodotus, and Mattathias to give and receive pledges of friendship.

**14:20** When the terms had been fully deliberated upon, and the leader had laid them before the multitude, and all were seen to be of one mind, they consented to the covenant.

**14:21** They set a day on which to meet privately. A seat was brought forward from each side; chairs of state were placed.

**14:22** Judas had armed men stationed at strategic points as a precaution against any sudden treachery on the enemy's part. The meeting was held in a proper manner.

**14:23** Nicanor stayed on in Jerusalem and did nothing irregular, but dismissed the crowds that had gathered to him.

**14:24** He kept Judas always at his side and was genuinely attached to the man.

**14:25** He urged him to marry and have children; Judas married, settled into a normal life, and shared in the common lot.

**14:26** But Alcimus, observing their goodwill for each other and taking hold of the covenants they had made, came to Demetrius and told him that Nicanor was being disloyal to the government, having appointed as his successor in Jewish affairs Judas, who was plotting against the kingdom.

**14:27** The king was provoked, and infuriated by the slanders of this most wicked man, wrote to Nicanor declaring his displeasure at the covenants and commanding him to send Maccabeus to Antioch as a prisoner without delay.

**14:28** When this reached Nicanor, he was troubled and deeply grieved that he would have to annul their agreements when the man had done nothing wrong.

**14:29** But since it was impossible to act contrary to the king, he watched for an opportunity to carry out the order by a stratagem.

**14:30** Maccabeus noticed that Nicanor was growing colder toward him and behaving more curtly than usual in their meetings, and concluded that this coolness boded nothing good. So he gathered a large number of his men and went into hiding from Nicanor.

**14:31** When Nicanor recognized that the man had cleverly outwitted him, he went to the great and holy temple while the priests were offering the regular sacrifices and commanded them to hand the man over.

**14:32** When they declared on oath that they did not know where the man was whom he sought,

**14:33** he stretched out his right hand toward the sanctuary and swore this oath: "If you do not deliver Judas to me as a prisoner, I will raze this shrine of God to the ground, tear down the altar, and erect here a magnificent temple to Dionysus."

**14:34** With that he departed. But the priests stretched out their hands toward heaven and called upon him who always fights for our nation, saying:

**14:35** "You, O Lord of all, who stand in need of nothing, were pleased to have a temple for your habitation among us.

**14:36** So now, O holy Lord of all holiness, keep undefiled to all ages this house that has so recently been purified."

**14:37** A certain Razis, one of the elders of Jerusalem, was denounced to Nicanor as a man who loved his compatriots and was held in the highest esteem — a man called father of the Jews on account of his goodwill toward them.

**14:38** For in the former times, when there was no intermingling with the Gentiles, he had been put on trial for Judaism and had committed body and soul with complete earnestness to Judaism.

**14:39** Nicanor, wishing to make his hostility toward the Jews openly apparent, sent more than five hundred soldiers to arrest him;

**14:40** for he reckoned that by seizing him he would strike a blow to the Jews.

**14:41** Now when the troops were on the point of taking the tower and were forcing the door of the courtyard and had called for fire to burn down the doors, Razis — surrounded on all sides — fell upon his own sword,

**14:42** choosing to die nobly rather than fall into the hands of sinners and suffer treatment unworthy of his noble birth.

**14:43** In his haste, however, he missed the stroke; and as the crowd was pressing in through the doors, he ran boldly up to the wall and threw himself down bravely into the crowd.

**14:44** But when they quickly drew back, he fell in the open space between them.

**14:45** Still breathing, and inflamed with spirit, he rose up; though blood was gushing from his wounds in streams, he ran through the crowd and climbed to the top of a sheer rock.

**14:46** Now entirely drained of blood, he tore out his entrails and hurled them with both hands at the crowd. Then, calling upon the Lord of life and spirit to restore them to him again, he died in this manner.
